questions.q: Into how many total sequential steps does the World Health Organization (WHO) divide the inpatient management of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM)?
options: A) 5 steps
B) 7 steps
C) 10 steps
D) 12 steps
questions.hint: 10 sequential steps across two phases.
questions.explanation: The WHO inpatient management protocol for Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) is organized into 10 sequential steps divided across two main phases: Stabilization and Rehabilitation.

questions.q: What are the two primary clinical phases of inpatient management for Severe Acute Malnutrition?
options: A) Acute Phase and Chronic Phase
B) Stabilization Phase and Rehabilitation Phase
C) Induction Phase and Maintenance Phase
D) Resuscitation Phase and Curative Phase
questions.hint: Stabilization Phase and Rehabilitation Phase.
questions.explanation: Inpatient SAM management consists of an initial Stabilization Phase (Days 1–7) focused on life-saving medical stabilization, followed by a Rehabilitation Phase focused on catch-up growth and developmental support.

questions.q: What starter therapeutic formula is specifically used during Step 7 (Start Cautious Feeding) of the Stabilization Phase?
options: C) Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF)
D) Full-strength cow's milk
questions.explanation: F-75 (containing 75 kcal/100 mL) is the starter formula designed to support metabolic recovery without overwhelming the child's physiological systems during initial stabilization.

questions.q: Which therapeutic food or formula is introduced during the Rehabilitation Phase to promote rapid 'catch-up' tissue growth?
options: B) ReSoMal
C) F-100 or Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF)
D) Clear glucose water alone
questions.hint: F-100 or Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF).
questions.explanation: F-100 (100 kcal/100 mL) or RUTF is introduced in the Rehabilitation Phase once appetite returns and edema resolves to supply high calories and protein for catch-up growth.

questions.q: What specialized oral rehydration solution is recommended for treating dehydration in children with Severe Acute Malnutrition?
options: A) Standard World Health Organization Oral Rehydration Solution (WHO-ORS)
B) ReSoMal (Rehydration Solution for Malnutrition)
C) Hypertonic 3% Saline
D) Plain tap water with table salt
questions.hint: ReSoMal (Rehydration Solution for Malnutrition).
questions.explanation: ReSoMal is specifically formulated with lower sodium content and higher potassium and sugar levels to meet the altered electrolyte needs of severely malnourished children.

questions.q: What is the core mnemonic introduced in the source to remember the 10 WHO steps of inpatient malnutrition management?
options: A) AEIOU TIPS
B) ABCDE-SAM
C) GHENT-MIF
D) PALS-SAM
questions.hint: GHENT-MIF.
questions.explanation: 'GHENT-MIF' is the memory aid used to recall the 10 WHO steps: Glucose, Heat, Electrolytes & Dehydration, Nutrition (starter), Treat Infection, Micronutrients, Increase Feeding, and Follow-up & Sensory Stimulation.

questions.q: What fundamental safety rule applies to Iron administration during the initial Stabilization Phase of SAM management?
options: A) Give high-dose IV iron on Day 1
B) Delay iron supplementation until the child is stabilized, edema has resolved, and weight gain has begun
C) Give oral iron together with starter formula F-75 from the first feed
D) Iron is completely contraindicated permanently in malnourished children
questions.hint: Delay iron until stabilized, edema is resolving, and weight gain has started.
questions.explanation: Iron must be withheld during the initial Stabilization Phase because unabsorbed free iron promotes bacterial proliferation and oxidative tissue damage; iron is added only during the Rehabilitation Phase.

questions.q: What critical restriction applies to routine Intravenous (IV) fluids during the management of dehydration in SAM?
options: A) IV fluids are mandatory for all children with SAM on admission
B) Routine IV fluids should be strictly avoided unless the child exhibits clinical signs of frank shock
C) Give 60 mL/kg normal saline boluses immediately to all edematous children
D) IV fluids should be given continuously over 48 hours to correct low blood pressure
questions.hint: Avoid routine IV fluids unless the child has signs of frank shock.
questions.explanation: Children with SAM have compromised myocardial function and expanded intracellular sodium; routine IV fluids easily trigger fatal volume overload and heart failure unless true shock is present.

questions.q: What assumption must be made regarding infections in a child presenting with Severe Acute Malnutrition?
options: A) Infections are absent if the child has no fever
B) Serious underlying bacterial infection must be assumed present even if classic signs like fever are absent, requiring prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics
C) Antibiotics should be withheld until blood culture results are returned after 5 days
D) Antibiotics are required only if white blood cell count is >20,000/µL
questions.hint: Assume serious bacterial infection is present even without fever; start broad-spectrum antibiotics.
questions.explanation: Severely malnourished children have impaired inflammatory responses and often fail to produce fever; systemic infections must be presumed and treated empirically with broad-spectrum antimicrobials.

questions.q: How does Severe Acute Malnutrition impact the immune system?
options: A) It causes primary genetic immunodeficiency
B) It causes a form of Secondary Immunodeficiency, increasing vulnerability to severe infections and sepsis
C) It enhances T-lymphocyte function
D) It has no effect on immunity
questions.hint: Causes secondary immunodeficiency and higher risk of severe infections/sepsis.
questions.explanation: Malnutrition impairs both cellular and humoral immunity, serving as a leading cause of secondary immunodeficiency that predisposes children to overwhelming sepsis.

questions.q: Under the WHO 10-step protocol, which steps are performed strictly during the initial Stabilization Phase (Days 1–7)?
options: A) Steps 1 to 7 (Hypoglycemia, Hypothermia, Dehydration, Electrolytes, Infection, Micronutrients, Starter Feeding)
B) Steps 8 to 10 only
C) Steps 1, 5, and 10 only
D) All 10 steps are performed simultaneously on Day 1
questions.hint: Steps 1 to 7 cover initial stabilization.
questions.explanation: Steps 1 through 7 constitute the Stabilization Phase aimed at life-saving stabilization, while Steps 8 through 10 constitute the Rehabilitation Phase.

questions.q: How frequently should small feeds (F-75) be administered to a severely malnourished child during the first few days of the Stabilization Phase?
options: A) Once every 6 hours
B) Every 2 to 3 hours, day and night
C) Only when the child cries for food
D) Twice daily after morning rounds
questions.hint: Every 2 to 3 hours, day and night.
questions.explanation: To prevent hypoglycemia and metabolic collapse, feeds must be given in small, precise volumes every 2 to 3 hours throughout both day and night.

questions.q: What specific electrolyte changes are characteristic of Severe Acute Malnutrition, requiring targeted correction in Step 4?
options: A) High intracellular potassium and low body sodium
B) Total body potassium and magnesium depletion, with excess intracellular sodium
C) Severe hyperkalemia and hypernatremia
D) Hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia
questions.hint: Low potassium and magnesium, with excess intracellular sodium.
questions.explanation: Malnutrition causes sodium-pump dysfunction leading to intracellular sodium accumulation, while total body stores of potassium and magnesium are markedly depleted.

questions.q: Why are standard loop diuretics (e.g., Furosemide) contraindicated for managing nutritional edema in Kwashiorkor?
options: A) Diuretics cause acute lung damage
B) Diuretics worsen electrolyte collapse and intravascular hypovolemia, risking fatal circulatory shock
C) Diuretics neutralize the effect of antibiotics
D) Diuretics convert kwashiorkor into marasmus
questions.hint: They worsen electrolyte imbalance and intravascular hypovolemia/shock.
questions.explanation: Edema in SAM results from capillary leak and hypoalbuminemia, not fluid overload; diuretics dangerously deplete intravascular volume and cause cardiovascular collapse.

questions.q: What clinical criteria signal that a child with SAM is ready to transition from the Stabilization Phase to the Rehabilitation Phase (Step 8)?
options: A) Return of appetite (eagerly taking feeds) and initiation of edema resolution
B) Complete 30-day stay in hospital regardless of appetite
C) Immediate doubling of body weight on Day 2
D) Ability to walk independently
questions.hint: Return of appetite and starting resolution of edema.
questions.explanation: The key indicators of stabilization are a restored appetite (passing the appetite test) and reduction or resolution of nutritional edema.

questions.q: What essential role does Step 9 (Provide sensory stimulation and emotional support) play in the WHO 10-step protocol?
options: A) It is optional and only used if nursing staff have extra time
B) It prevents long-term neurodevelopmental delay and emotional trauma through structured play, loving care, and caregiver involvement
C) It replaces the need for starter formula F-75
D) It reduces the required antibiotic dosage
questions.hint: Prevents neurodevelopmental delay and emotional trauma through play and caregiver care.
questions.explanation: Malnutrition severely affects cognitive development; sensory stimulation and emotional bonding are essential components of holistic recovery.

questions.q: What micronutrients should be routinely administered during Step 6 of the Stabilization Phase?
options: A) Iron and Calcium only
B) High-dose Vitamin A, Folic Acid, Zinc, and Copper (with iron delayed)
C) Vitamin D and Vitamin K only
D) Intravenous Vitamin C alone
questions.hint: Vitamin A, folic acid, zinc, and copper (hold iron early).
questions.explanation: Baseline micronutrient replenishment requires Vitamin A, folic acid, zinc, and copper to restore cellular function and mucosal repair, while iron is held.

questions.q: In the GHENT-MIF mnemonic, what does the letter 'H' represent?
options: A) Hemoglobin optimization
B) Heat (Treat or prevent hypothermia)
C) Hydration with hypertonic saline
D) Hepatic enzyme monitoring
questions.hint: Heat (prevent/treat hypothermia).
questions.explanation: In GHENT-MIF, 'H' stands for Heat, representing Step 2 of the WHO protocol: treating and preventing hypothermia through thermal care.

questions.q: How is uncomplicated Severe Acute Malnutrition managed in community health settings according to standard guidelines?
options: A) Immediate admission for 6 weeks of IV fluids
B) Outpatient care using Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and routine oral antibiotics
C) Complete fluid restriction without feeding
D) High-dose steroid therapy at home
questions.hint: Outpatient care with RUTF and routine oral antibiotics.
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated SAM (children with good appetite and no severe medical complications) is managed safely in outpatient community settings using RUTF.

questions.q: What is the rationale for continuing breastfeeding during the management of Severe Acute Malnutrition in infants?
options: A) Breastfeeding provides essential immunological protection, hydration, and comfort alongside therapeutic feeds
B) Breastfeeding should be stopped to allow full uptake of F-75
C) Breast milk causes severe lactose intolerance in SAM
D) Breastfeeding is permitted only after 3 months of rehabilitation
questions.hint: Provides immune protection, hydration, and comfort alongside therapeutic feeds.
questions.explanation: Breastfeeding should always be continued on demand in malnourished infants alongside therapeutic starter feeds.

questions.q: What temperature threshold defines Hypothermia in a child evaluated for Severe Acute Malnutrition?
options: A) Axillary temperature < 35.0°C or Rectal temperature < 35.5°C
B) Axillary temperature < 36.5°C
C) Temperature < 37.0°C
D) Temperature < 33.0°C only
questions.hint: Axillary < 35.0°C or rectal < 35.5°C.
questions.explanation: Hypothermia in SAM is defined as an axillary temperature under 35.0°C (or rectal under 35.5°C), reflecting impaired thermogenesis and high risk of mortality.

questions.q: What blood glucose level defines Hypoglycemia in a child with Severe Acute Malnutrition?
options: A) Blood glucose < 3.0 mmol/L (< 54 mg/dL)
B) Blood glucose < 4.0 mmol/L
C) Blood glucose < 5.0 mmol/L
D) Blood glucose < 1.5 mmol/L only
questions.hint: Blood glucose < 3.0 mmol/L (< 54 mg/dL).
questions.explanation: In SAM, hypoglycemia is defined as blood glucose < 3.0 mmol/L (or < 54 mg/dL), a lower threshold than in healthy children due to depleted glycogen reserves.

questions.q: What non-pharmacological interventions are essential to prevent and manage hypothermia in a hospitalized child with SAM?
options: A) Cold water sponge bathing
B) Keeping the room warm (25–28°C), avoiding drafts, utilizing Kangaroo Mother Care (skin-to-skin contact), and capping/wrapping the head
C) Continuous fan ventilation
D) Rapid infusion of ice-cold IV saline
questions.hint: Warm room (25–28°C), avoid drafts, Kangaroo care, and cover head.
questions.explanation: Prevention of radiant and convective heat loss via warm environment, clothing, head coverage, and skin-to-skin contact is critical for maintaining body temperature.

questions.q: Why is assessing dehydration by skin turgor alone unreliable in children with Marasmus or Kwashiorkor?
options: A) Because skin turgor is always normal in SAM
B) In Marasmus, loss of subcutaneous fat causes skin tenting without true dehydration; in Kwashiorkor, edema masks skin turgor loss
C) Because skin turgor cannot be performed on pediatric limbs
D) Because dehydration does not occur in malnourished children
questions.hint: Marasmus loses fat (false tenting); kwashiorkor has edema (masks signs).
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous fat loss in marasmus produces false-positive skin tenting, while nutritional edema in kwashiorkor obscures fluid status, making standard physical signs of dehydration unreliable.

questions.q: What signs should be closely monitored to detect Fluid Overload during rehydration or feeding of a child with SAM?
options: A) Increased urine output alone
B) Rising respiratory rate, worsening tachypnea, chest retractions, neck vein engorgement, and increasing liver enlargement
C) Falling heart rate and warm extremities
D) Dry mucous membranes
questions.hint: Rising respiratory rate/retractions, neck vein distension, and enlarging liver.
questions.explanation: Overhydration in SAM leads to rapid cardiac decompensation; serial monitoring of respiratory rate, effort, jugular venous pressure, and liver size detects early pulmonary edema.

questions.q: What metabolic composition renders ReSoMal superior to standard WHO-ORS for dehydrating SAM patients?
options: A) ReSoMal has higher sodium and lower potassium
B) ReSoMal has reduced sodium (~45 mmol/L), increased potassium (~40 mmol/L), increased magnesium, and added sugar
C) ReSoMal contains 0% glucose
D) ReSoMal is identical to normal saline
questions.hint: Lower sodium, higher potassium/magnesium, and added sugar.
questions.explanation: ReSoMal contains less sodium to prevent hypernatremic fluid overload, and higher potassium/magnesium to replace intracellular electrolyte deficits.

questions.q: What initial management is indicated if a child with SAM presents with confirmed Hypoglycemia (blood glucose < 3.0 mmol/L) and is conscious?
options: A) Give 50 mL of 10% glucose or sucrose solution orally or by nasogastric tube immediately, followed by early feeding
B) Administer 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV bolus
C) Withhold all food for 12 hours
D) Give cold plain water
questions.hint: 50 mL of 10% glucose/sucrose orally or by NG tube, then start feeding.
questions.explanation: Conscious hypoglycemic SAM children should receive 50 mL of 10% glucose/sucrose orally or via NG tube, with immediate continuation of small frequent feeds.

questions.q: What clinical indication permits the cautious administration of Intravenous Fluids in a child with SAM?
options: A) Presence of mild diarrhea without lethargy
B) Clear clinical signs of Septic or Hypovolemic Shock (lethargy/unconsciousness, weak/absent pulse, cold extremities, and delayed CRT)
C) Presence of Grade +3 nutritional edema
D) Routine admission requirement
questions.hint: Only with clear signs of shock.
questions.explanation: IV fluids are strictly reserved for severe shock with circulatory collapse due to the high risk of iatrogenic heart failure.

questions.q: Why is extra Potassium provided throughout the management of Severe Acute Malnutrition?
options: A) To increase blood pressure
B) To correct total body potassium depletion, restore cellular membrane potentials, and prevent cardiac arrhythmias
C) To induce vomiting
D) To prevent iron absorption
questions.hint: Corrects total body potassium depletion and supports cardiac/cellular function.
questions.explanation: Severe intracellular potassium depletion affects cardiac, intestinal, and skeletal muscle function; potassium supplementation (3–4 mmol/kg/day) is essential.

questions.q: In the GHENT-MIF mnemonic, what does the letter 'E' highlight regarding clinical management?
options: A) Early Emergency Intubation
B) Electrolytes (correct imbalances) & Dehydration management (prefer ReSoMal, restrict sodium)
C) Exercise therapy
D) Enema administration
questions.hint: Electrolytes and dehydration management.
questions.explanation: 'E' in GHENT-MIF stands for Electrolyte correction and cautious Dehydration management without routine IV fluids.

questions.q: What is the caloric density and main therapeutic objective of starter formula F-75?
options: A) 100 kcal/100 mL; intended for rapid weight gain
B) 75 kcal/100 mL; intended to restore cellular function and metabolic stability without overloading cardiac or renal capacity
C) 150 kcal/100 mL; intended for muscle hypertrophy
D) 50 kcal/100 mL; intended for fluid restriction
questions.hint: 75 kcal/100 mL to stabilize metabolism without overloading heart/kidneys.
questions.explanation: F-75 provides 75 kcal per 100 mL; its reduced protein and calorie composition prevents refeeding syndrome and cardiac failure during initial stabilization.

questions.q: What is the caloric density of F-100 formula used during the Rehabilitation Phase?
options: A) 75 kcal/100 mL
B) 100 kcal/100 mL
C) 200 kcal/100 mL
D) 500 kcal/100 mL
questions.hint: 100 kcal/100 mL.
questions.explanation: F-100 formula provides 100 kcal per 100 mL, supplying the high energy density required for rapid tissue catch-up growth.

questions.q: Why is broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy routinely administered to ALL children admitted with SAM, even in the absence of fever?
options: A) To satisfy hospital billing protocols
B) Because severely malnourished children have defective immune systems that fail to produce localized signs or fever despite severe, life-threatening bacterial infections
C) Antibiotics act as anabolic growth stimulants
D) Antibiotics increase appetite directly
questions.hint: Immunocompromised SAM children often lack fever despite serious bacterial infection.
questions.explanation: Immunocompromise in SAM dampens fever and inflammatory signs; occult bacteremia and infections are present in nearly all admitted SAM patients.

questions.q: What specific physiological danger is triggered if high-dose Iron is administered during the first 2 days of SAM stabilization?
options: A) Iron induces severe hypoglycemia
B) Free unbound iron promotes rapid bacterial replication and generates harmful free radicals, increasing early mortality
C) Iron destroys vitamin A in the gut
D) Iron causes immediate renal stones
questions.hint: Free iron can fuel bacterial growth and cause oxidative free-radical damage.
questions.explanation: Malnourished children have low transferrin levels; early iron remains free in blood, feeding pathogenic bacteria and causing oxidative tissue destruction.

questions.q: When should Iron supplementation finally be initiated in a child treated for SAM?
options: A) On admission Day 1
B) During the Rehabilitation Phase (Step 8) once the child demonstrates active weight gain and good appetite
C) Only after 1 year of discharge
D) Iron is never given
questions.hint: In the rehabilitation phase when appetite returns and weight gain begins.
questions.explanation: Iron is safely added to feeds during the Rehabilitation Phase when protein synthesis and erythropoiesis are actively occurring.

questions.q: What initial empirical antibiotic strategy is recommended for uncomplicated SAM vs. severe complicated SAM?
options: A) Uncomplicated: Oral Amoxicillin; Complicated: IV Ampicillin + Gentamicin
B) Uncomplicated: IV Vancomycin; Complicated: Oral Nystatin
C) Uncomplicated: No antibiotics; Complicated: Oral Metronidazole alone
D) Uncomplicated: IV Ciprofloxacin; Complicated: Oral Paracetamol
questions.hint: Oral amoxicillin for uncomplicated; IV ampicillin + gentamicin for complicated.
questions.explanation: Outpatient uncomplicated SAM receives routine oral Amoxicillin; inpatient complicated SAM requires parenteral broad-spectrum coverage (IV Ampicillin + Gentamicin).

questions.q: What essential role does Zinc supplementation play during the recovery phase of SAM?
options: A) Zinc lowers serum potassium
B) Zinc promotes mucosal healing, restores immune function, and supports enzymatic growth pathways
C) Zinc replaces the need for F-75
D) Zinc prevents hypothermia
questions.hint: Supports mucosal repair, immunity, and growth pathways.
questions.explanation: Zinc is a critical cofactor for protein synthesis, cell division, gut mucosal integrity, and immune reconstitution.

questions.q: In the GHENT-MIF mnemonic, what does the letter 'N' represent?
options: A) Neurological examination
B) Nutrition (Starter feeding with F-75)
C) Normal saline bolus
D) Niacin high-dose therapy
questions.hint: Nutrition (starter feeding with F-75).
questions.explanation: 'N' in GHENT-MIF stands for starting cautious Nutrition using F-75 starter formula (Step 7).

questions.q: In the GHENT-MIF mnemonic, what does the letter 'M' represent?
options: A) Muscle biopsy
B) Micronutrient supplementation (with iron delayed)
C) Mantoux testing
D) Morphine administration
questions.hint: Micronutrients (delaying iron early).
questions.explanation: 'M' in GHENT-MIF stands for Micronutrients (Vitamin A, zinc, copper, folic acid), reminding clinicians to hold iron early.

questions.q: In the GHENT-MIF mnemonic, what does the letter 'I' represent?
options: A) Intravenous hydration
B) Increase feeding for catch-up growth (transition to F-100 / RUTF)
C) Insulin infusion
D) Isolation precautions
questions.hint: Increase feeding for catch-up growth (F-100 or RUTF).
questions.explanation: 'I' in GHENT-MIF stands for Increase feeding (Step 8: catch-up growth with F-100 or RUTF).

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy with severe marasmus is admitted to the stabilization ward with axillary temperature 34.8°C and blood glucose 2.2 mmol/L, lethargic but conscious. Identify the emergencies, immediate 30-minute management, and GHENT-MIF letters.
options: A) Severe Anemia and Sepsis; Give IV blood transfusion; Letters A & B

B) Hypothermia (< 35.0°C) and Hypoglycemia (< 3.0 mmol/L); Administer 50 mL of 10% oral/NG glucose solution, provide immediate warm re-feeding (F-75), wrap head, and apply skin-to-skin care; Letters G (Glucose) & H (Heat)
C) Hyperglycemia and Dehydration; Give IV insulin and IV normal saline; Letters I & D
D) Kwashiorkor; Give oral furosemide; Letter F
questions.hint: Hypoglycemia + hypothermia (G & H) -> 10% glucose, warmth/Kangaroo care, F-75.
questions.explanation: Blood glucose < 3.0 mmol/L and temp < 35.0°C represent Hypoglycemia and Hypothermia (Steps 1 & 2 / G & H). Management requires 10% glucose, F-75, and thermal care.

questions.q: An 18-month-old girl with Kwashiorkor (+3 pitting edema) has lethargy and watery diarrhea; a resident orders 20 mL/kg IV normal saline and 40 mg IV furosemide. Critique the plan, note complications, and state proper Step 3/4 care.
options: A) The plan is correct and evidence-based.

B) The plan is dangerous; routine IV fluids cause fatal heart failure/pulmonary edema, and diuretics exacerbate electrolyte collapse/shock; manage with oral/NG ReSoMal, extra potassium/magnesium, and restrict sodium without diuretics
C) Give double-dose furosemide with hypertonic saline
D) Administer high-dose albumin IV bolus
questions.hint: Avoid routine IV fluids and diuretics; use ReSoMal + potassium/magnesium and restrict sodium.
questions.explanation: Routine IV fluids and diuretics are major pitfalls in SAM. IV fluids trigger heart failure, while diuretics trigger hypovolemic shock. Dehydration requires ReSoMal, potassium, and sodium restriction (E in GHENT-MIF).

questions.q: A 3-year-old child with severe marasmic-kwashiorkor is on F-75 on Day 2 when oral iron is added for pallor. Why is early iron risky, what is the rule, and when is iron started under GHENT-MIF?
options: A) Iron causes severe diarrhea; Give iron IV instead

B) Early iron provides free unbound iron that promotes bacterial overgrowth, sepsis, and oxidative free-radical damage; Iron must be delayed until Step 8 (Rehabilitation Phase / Letter I) when edema resolves and weight gain begins
C) Iron prevents vitamin A absorption; Give iron at 5 years of age
D) Iron is completely safe at all times
questions.hint: Free iron fuels bacteria and free radicals; delay until rehabilitation/catch-up growth (Letter I).
questions.explanation: Early iron administration is a critical pitfall. Unbound iron fuels bacterial proliferation and causes free radical injury. Iron is given only during catch-up growth (M & I in GHENT-MIF).

questions.q: A 15-month-old with SAM has temp 36.6°C and no cough, but is lethargic, hypopneic, and hypocirculatory. Does lack of fever rule out infection, which step/letter applies, and what antibiotics are given?
options: A) Yes; infection is ruled out; Withhold antibiotics
B) No; SAM children cannot generate fever due to immunosuppression; Step 5 (Treat Infection / Letter T) mandates starting broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., IV Ampicillin + Gentamicin) immediately
C) Give oral antipyretics only
D) Perform lumbar puncture and wait 7 days before starting therapy
questions.hint: No fever does not rule out infection in SAM (Letter T) -> start broad-spectrum antibiotics.
questions.explanation: Absence of fever does NOT rule out infection in SAM due to secondary immunodeficiency. Step 5 (T in GHENT-MIF) mandates empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics.

questions.q: A 2-year-old with SAM has completed 5 days on F-75; edema is gone, appetite is strong, and all F-75 feeds are finished. What milestone is met, what is the feeding transition (Step 8 / Letter I), and what is the catch-up feed?
options: A) Patient has failed treatment; Re-start stabilization with ReSoMal
B) Patient has achieved stabilization and is ready for the Rehabilitation Phase; transition gradually from F-75 to F-100 (or RUTF) over 48 hours to rebuild wasted tissues
C) Discharge home immediately without further feeding
D) Switch to low-calorie clear broths
questions.hint: Stabilized -> transition from F-75 to F-100 or RUTF for catch-up growth.
questions.explanation: Restored appetite and resolved edema signal readiness for Rehabilitation (Step 8 / Letter I). Feeding is transitioned from F-75 to F-100/RUTF to achieve catch-up growth.

questions.q: During oral ReSoMal rehydration of a malnourished child, respiratory rate rises from 30 to 55/min, lung base crackles appear, and liver enlarges by 3 cm. Identify the complication and immediate action.
options: A) Dehydration is worsening; Increase ReSoMal rate
B) Fluid Overload and Early Pulmonary Edema; Stop ReSoMal/IV fluids immediately, assess airway, and monitor closely
C) Pneumothorax; Perform chest tube drainage
D) Hypoglycemia; Give 50% dextrose IV
questions.hint: Tachypnea, crackles, and enlarging liver = fluid overload/pulmonary edema -> stop fluids immediately.
questions.explanation: Tachypnea, basal lung crackles, and liver enlargement indicate fluid overload and incipient heart failure. All fluids must be stopped immediately.

questions.q: Match each letter of GHENT-MIF to its clinical meaning in SAM management.
options: A) G=Glucose, H=Heat, E=Electrolytes/Dehydration, N=Nutrition (F-75), T=Treat Infection, M=Micronutrients (no early iron), I=Increase Feeding (F-100/RUTF), F=Follow-up & Sensory Stimulation
B) G=Gastric lavage, H=Heparin, E=Epinephrine, N=Niacin, T=Tetanus, M=Morphine, I=Insulin, F=Furosemide
C) G=Gentamicin, H=Hydrocortisone, E=Erythromycin, N=Neostigmine, T=Theophylline, M=Mannitol, I=Ibuprofen, F=Fluid bolus
D) G=Growth hormone, H=Haloperidol, E=Enalapril, N=Nifedipine, T=Thyroxine, M=Metformin, I=Iodine, F=Folic acid
questions.hint: Glucose, Heat, Electrolytes/Dehydration, Nutrition, Treat infection, Micronutrients, Increase feeding, Follow-up & stimulation.
questions.explanation: GHENT-MIF summarizes the 10 WHO steps in exact sequence: Glucose, Heat, Electrolytes/Dehydration, Nutrition, Treat Infection, Micronutrients, Increase Feeding, Follow-up & Sensory Stimulation.

questions.q: Why is standard WHO-ORS high in sodium (75 mmol/L) unsafe for routine rehydration in SAM patients without shock?
options: A) It causes severe diarrhea
B) Malnourished children have excess intracellular sodium due to Na+/K+ ATPase pump failure; high-sodium fluids cause fluid retention, hypernatremia, and acute heart failure
C) High sodium neutralizes F-75
D) It causes hypothermia
questions.hint: Excess intracellular sodium from pump failure + extra sodium = water retention and heart failure.
questions.explanation: In SAM, cellular pump failure traps sodium inside cells. Giving high-sodium ORS causes water retention, expansion of intravascular volume, and fatal heart failure.

questions.q: What discharge planning and follow-up measures comprise Step 10 (Letter F in GHENT-MIF)?
options: A) Discontinue all follow-up visits upon discharge
B) Caregiver education on appropriate feeding, hygiene, and danger signs; provision of RUTF; linkage to community health facilities; and scheduled outpatient follow-up
C) Permanent hospitalization until 18 years of age
D) Oral steroid maintenance at home
questions.hint: Caregiver education, RUTF supply, community linkage, and outpatient follow-up.
questions.explanation: Step 10 (F in GHENT-MIF) focuses on caregiver empowerment, hygiene/nutrition education, RUTF supply, and establishing outpatient follow-up to prevent relapse.

questions.q: Outline the master stabilization and recovery sequence for a 1-year-old with severe SAM, hypothermia, lethargy, and loose stools: (1) first 2 hours, (2) Days 1–7, and (3) Rehabilitation Phase.
options: A) 1. High-dose IV fluids, IV furosemide, oral iron; 2. Discharge home; 3. Readmit after 1 month

B) 1. Check blood glucose and temperature; give 10% glucose solution, provide thermal care (Kangaroo care/warm blankets), start F-75 starter feed every 2–3 hours; 2. Provide ReSoMal for diarrhea, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, supplement potassium/magnesium and micronutrients (hold iron); 3. Transition to F-100/RUTF for catch-up growth, provide sensory stimulation, and prepare for discharge (GHENT-MIF protocol)
C) 1. Give IV normal saline 60 mL/kg bolus; 2. Give oral iron; 3. Stop feeding
D) 1. Cold water bath; 2. Fasting for 7 days; 3. IV amino acids
questions.hint: 0–2h: glucose, warmth, F-75; Days 1–7: ReSoMal, antibiotics, K+/Mg2+/micronutrients (no early iron); Rehab: F-100/RUTF, stimulation, follow-up.
questions.explanation: Master management follows GHENT-MIF: immediate glucose/heat/starter F-75 (0–2h), ReSoMal/potassium/antibiotics/micronutrients (Days 1–7), followed by F-100/RUTF catch-up growth, stimulation, and discharge planning.
